sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
The 2015 Tunisian Solar Plan set a 14% renewable share of electricity generation for 2020 and 30% for 2030 (SRC-TG-192). ONEM reported 2.6% in 2020 excluding self-producers (SRC-TG-194). Later ONEM series include self-produced PV: 5.2% in 2024, 5.3% in 2025, and 8.3% for January-September 2026 (SRC-TG-193, SRC-TG-100). These are not a fully comparable uninterrupted series: ONEM began counting renewable self-production in January 2024, and concession solar plants in the IPP series from December 2025 (SRC-TG-100).

Utility-scale deployment has progressed slowly. The 500 MW solar concession tender closed in July 2019; the ministry announced results on 20 December 2019, while project agreements were approved in December 2021 (SRC-TG-195). ONEM reports that the Kairouan 100 MW plant entered service in December 2025, Sidi Bouzid's 50 MW in January 2026 and Tozeur's 50 MW in the first quarter of 2026; Gafsa's 100 MW is planned to enter service in 2027 (SRC-TG-193). ONEM's later September 2026 bulletin dates Sidi Bouzid and Tozeur to April 2026 and gives no service date for Gafsa, which is at financial close (SRC-TG-100). These dates establish the sequence, not an award-to-operation duration for each project. Of 54 authorisation projects granted agreements in principle for 261 MW during 2017-2020, 15 projects (four 10 MW and eleven 1 MW; 51 MW total) were in service by 2025 (SRC-TG-193).

Rooftop and other self-production expanded faster. ONEM reports about 420 MW of low-voltage self-production installed by end-2025, and 543 MW of residential rooftop PV by end-September 2026 (SRC-TG-193, SRC-TG-100). The 2015 Plan scheduled 392 MW of net-metering PV for households and business buildings by 2025; its household Prosol Elec component was 240 MW for 2025 and 390 MW for 2030 (SRC-TG-192). The plan values cover different categories and years from the later ONEM totals, so these comparisons show scale and direction rather than a like-for-like programme evaluation.

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
The evidence identifies several constraints, but does not quantify their contribution to individual project delays:

- **Offtaker exposure and project finance (policy/economic).** Under the 2015 law, authorised domestic-market producers sell all output exclusively to the public utility (art. 22); self-producers originally could sell surpluses only to it (art. 9). The 2019 amendment replaced article 9, allowing eligible self-producers to sell to consumers above a specified subscribed-capacity threshold while retaining the surplus-sale route to the public utility (SRC-TG-191, SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203). The amendment therefore qualifies, rather than eliminates, STEG's central role in utility-scale PPAs. The 2023 policy paper says banks' main security is the STEG electricity-sale contract, reports investor requests for comfort letters and says they were issued in August 2022 (SRC-TG-195). The World Bank states that STEG's difficult finances as main buyer hindered private renewable investment (SRC-TG-105); this is a reported barrier, not a quantified causal estimate. STEG's finances are treated separately in FND-TG-161.
- **Administrative process (institutional).** Articles 12 and 13 of the 2015 law provide annual-needs notice, technical-commission review and parliamentary steps for domestic authorisations and concessions. Article 25's parliamentary approval by law concerns export concessions, not the domestic projects discussed here (SRC-TG-191). Law 2019-47 amended article 9, not articles 12-13 (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203). The 2016 implementing order (Order n° 1123 of 24 August 2016) sets application, commission, grid-study and project-development stages (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203). A 2023 policy paper reports that procedures take at least three years before production starts in its Arabic text (PDF p. 20) and at least two years in its English text (PDF p. 5); the two texts conflict and no other source settles it. The paper does not identify a sample or project-level durations, so this is a reported assessment rather than a measured national average (SRC-TG-195). The same paper says the ministry handled authorisations through calls within annual needs quotas (SRC-TG-195).
- **Grid connection (technical/economic).** The IRENA-ANME report says STEG grid works face long public-procurement procedures, and the 2023 policy paper identifies the ageing transmission grid and lengthy connection processes as barriers (SRC-TG-106, SRC-TG-195). Article 8 of the 2015 law generally places connection and needed reinforcement costs on the producer. Article 21 of Decree-law 2022-68 added an exception allowing the public body to bear them when the State proposed the site (SRC-TG-191, SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203). The sources do not quantify connection waits or curtailment.
- **Land and local acceptance (institutional).** The policy paper says land access was not prepared in the 2017-2022 programme, reports difficulty using agricultural land classified as conservation zones, and links some land problems to limited local-community involvement and high local employment expectations (SRC-TG-106, SRC-TG-195). The 2019 and 2022 amendments provide for renewable projects on private land and authorised state or local land; the 2022 text states that such projects do not require a change in agricultural land allocation (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203). These provisions do not establish how often land access blocked a project or the scale of local opposition.
- **Finance, bidding and governance (economic/institutional).** The policy paper reports very low bids by some inexperienced or speculative entrants followed by financing difficulties. The World Bank also cites early market learning, post-COVID cost increases, bureaucratic inefficiencies and financial risks (SRC-TG-195, SRC-TG-105). The policy paper records investors' request for an independent electricity regulator because of overlapping STEG roles, but the evidence does not show that regulator absence caused particular projects to fail (SRC-TG-195).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- **Electricity shares and targets.** ONEM's key figures report renewable shares (hydro, wind and solar) of 2.8% in 2019 and 2.6% in 2020 excluding self-producers (SRC-TG-194). IRENA reports 6% for 2023 (SRC-TG-190). ONEM's mix chart gives hydro, wind and solar shares that sum to 5.2% in 2024 and 5.3% in 2025 including self-produced PV (SRC-TG-193), and 8.3% for January-September 2026 including self-production (SRC-TG-100). ONEM says self-production enters the series from January 2024 and concession plants from December 2025 (SRC-TG-100). A September 2026 press article attributes 9.2% at end-June 2026 to ONEM, but this remains tier C sourced reporting (SRC-TG-199). The 2015 Plan itself gives a 14% interim target for 2020; the press article reports 12% as the target adopted in 2016 and 3.1% as the 2020 outcome, unlike ONEM's 2.6% excluding self-production (SRC-TG-192, SRC-TG-199, SRC-TG-194). Keep those source and accounting differences explicit. The 2026 bulletin says renewable output rose 66% in January-September 2026 year over year (SRC-TG-100).
- **Installed capacity and scope.** IRENA reports 1,086 MW at end-2024, representing 15% of total capacity in its table (SRC-TG-190). The World Bank reports 516 MW at end-2023, 45% STEG-owned and 55% private (SRC-TG-105). ONEM reports 339 MW in 2024 and 463 MW in 2025 in the net generating fleet excluding self-production (SRC-TG-193). These are estimates with different dates and scopes. The proposed explanation that the difference is mostly rooftop/self-production is plausible but not demonstrated by the cited source records; the capacity totals should remain unreconciled.
- **2018 concession tender.** The 500 MW PV tender on State-proposed sites closed in July 2019. IRENA reports five bids with prices of 2.44-2.86 US cents/kWh; the 2023 policy paper reports eight financial offers, with a best offer of about 2.4 US cents/kWh (SRC-TG-106, SRC-TG-195). These descriptions may refer to different stages and do not establish a direct contradiction. The policy paper says results were announced on 20 December 2019 and the five project agreements approved by decree-laws in December 2021; do not describe that as a verified award-to-approval interval (SRC-TG-195). ONEM's project table reports Kairouan 100 MW in service December 2025; Sidi Bouzid 50 MW January 2026; Tozeur 50 MW in service in Q1 2026; Gafsa 100 MW planned for 2027 and its agreement signed 8 May 2024; it lists a 200 MW Tataouine lot without a project status (SRC-TG-193). Separately, the World Bank's April 2025 appraisal document says 200 MW was under construction and 300 MW nearing financial close (SRC-TG-105).
- **Later tenders and authorisations.** ONEM reports that the 2022 1,700 MW tender included 800 MW PV on private sites, 600 MW wind on private sites and 300 MW at two State sites; project agreements for 300 MW and 198 MW were signed on 24 March 2025, with service expected in 2027 for the 300 MW projects (SRC-TG-193). The World Bank separately says a 500 MW solar round was awarded in December 2024 at 3.1-3.3 US cents/kWh (SRC-TG-105). ONEM records 54 agreements in principle for 261 MW across four authorisation calls in 2017-2020, of which 15 projects totaling 51 MW were in service by 2025; its fifth call (October 2024-June 2025) produced 186 agreements in principle for 288 MW (SRC-TG-193). ONEM reports 124 MW of solar under authorisation and concession entered production in 2025 (SRC-TG-193). Agreements and planned service dates are not treated as operating capacity.
- **Self-production.** The 2023 policy paper describes Prosol Elec support as a 30% grant plus seven-year bank loans repaid through the STEG bill; it reports more than 600 installer firms and capacity above 200 MW at end-2022 (SRC-TG-195). The World Bank's April 2025 appraisal document describes 250 MW installed “to date” under the residential and commercial rooftop programme; the measurement date is not separately specified (SRC-TG-105). ONEM reports about 420 MW low-voltage self-production at end-2025 and 70 MW of medium- and high-voltage projects in service by end-2025 (SRC-TG-193); by end-September 2026, it reports 543 MW residential rooftop PV and 150 MW at medium/high voltage (SRC-TG-100). These labels have different sector and voltage scopes. IRENA's report says about 11.3 MWp was connected on the low-voltage grid at end-2019, while the 2015 Plan scheduled 30 MW of net-metering PV by 2015; these are an actual and a plan value, not a direct statistical contradiction, and scope equivalence is not demonstrated (SRC-TG-106, SRC-TG-192). ONEM's 2025 key figures report 721 GWh self-production and 37 GWh solar IPP output in 2025; the September 2026 bulletin's full-year 2025 column gives 81 GWh for solar IPPs. Preserve the unresolved ONEM discrepancy without assuming a reconciliation (SRC-TG-193, SRC-TG-100).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Confidence is medium. Outcome evidence is mainly tier A ONEM and IRENA reporting, but some data are partial-year, differently scoped or methodologically discontinuous; the 37 versus 81 GWh ONEM figures remain unreconciled. The causal mechanisms are described by tier B policy and World Bank reports and are rarely quantified at project level. The FNF policy paper was co-written with ministry officials, so its account is near-official but still a report rather than project-level administrative data (SRC-TG-195). The tier C June 2026 share is clearly attributed as press reporting. The trend is improving because ONEM reports a 66% year-over-year increase in renewable output in Jan-Sep 2026 and concession plants began entering service, while reported shares remain below the 2015 Plan's 30% 2030 goal; the accounting break and distinct denominators limit direct comparison (SRC-TG-100, SRC-TG-193, SRC-TG-192).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Agriculture.** Renewable projects interact with agricultural land rules, and sources report land-access barriers. The 2022 amendment permits projects on private or authorised public land and states they do not require a change in agricultural land allocation; no source quantifies agricultural land used or sought for renewable projects (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203, SRC-TG-195).
- **Energy finances.** The World Bank identifies STEG's financial condition as a barrier to private renewable investment; see FND-TG-161 for the utility's finances (SRC-TG-105).

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Law n° 2015-12 of 11 May 2015 and its amendment Law n° 2019-47 of 29 May 2019 (corporate PPAs) (SRC-TG-191, SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203).
- Prosol Elec residential rooftop programme (ANME, STEG, FTE grant and on-bill loans) (SRC-TG-195, SRC-TG-106).
- Concession tenders: 500 MW (2018-2019) and 1,700 MW (2022, AO-01/02/03-2022) (SRC-TG-193).
- Fifth authorisation call (2024-2025) and ministry plans to set tariffs itself and screen project readiness (bank approval, permits, site, guarantee) (SRC-TG-193, SRC-TG-195).
- Decree-law n° 2022-68 of 19 October 2022 (renewable project land provisions) (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-202, SRC-TG-203).
- Draft law creating an independent electricity regulator (SRC-TG-195, SRC-TG-105).
- World Bank TERI technical assistance and TEREG programme (SRC-TG-196, SRC-TG-105).
- ANME help desk and proposed single online platform for permits (SRC-TG-106).
- Proposed pre-allocated land bank with grid connection prepared before tenders (SRC-TG-195).

sections.heading: Verification status
sections.content:
Article 7 of Law 2019-47 replaced article 9 on self-production. Article 14 of the original 2016 decree sets domestic authorisation ceilings of 10 MW for photovoltaic and 30 MW for wind projects. Neither provision measures the contribution of permitting to delays. Dated outcomes, accounts of individual project delays and general legal requirements are reported separately (SRC-TG-200, SRC-TG-201, SRC-TG-191).

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Originals checked: FNF policy paper 2023 (SRC-TG-195), English PDF p. 5 (at least two years) and Arabic section 3.1.3, PDF p. 20 (at least three years); World Bank TEREG appraisal document, paragraph 8 (STEG finances) and background (516 MW) (SRC-TG-105); IRENA energy profile (SRC-TG-190), p. 2 (1,086 MW) and p. 3 (6% in 2023); ONEM Chiffres cles 2025 (SRC-TG-193), p. 17 (463 and 339 MW, 124 MW), p. 18 mix charts, pp. 39-40 project and authorisation tables (420 MW; 54 agreements for 261 MW; 15 projects in service; 70 MW medium and high voltage); ONEM Chiffres cles 2020 (SRC-TG-194, 2.6%); Solar Plan 2015 (SRC-TG-192, 392, 240 and 390 MW and the 14% and 30% targets); ONEM Conjoncture energetique, September 2026 (SRC-TG-100, 8.3% and 543 MW). Corrections made: the procedure duration is now reported as three years in the Arabic text and two years in the English text of the same paper (root cause, body text and a second indicator); the 5.2% and 5.3% shares are described as sums of the chart's hydro, wind and solar shares; the later September 2026 project dates are noted; the article-level legal provisions and the Article 14 ceilings were added to data_gaps as not independently reopened. No quantified split of financing, procedural and project-specific delay exists in any source opened, and the record makes no such claim. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

resolvedSources.extracts:
JORT p. 926, Article premier:

> La présente loi a pour objectif de définir le régime juridique relatif à la réalisation des projets de production d'électricité à partir de sources d'énergie renouvelables, soit pour l'autoconsommation ou pour répondre aux besoins de la consommation locale ou en vue de l'exportation, et ce, nonobstant les dispositions du décret-loi n° 62-8 du 3 avril 1962 relatif à la création et l'organisation de la Société tunisienne de l'électricité et du gaz, ratifié par la loi n° 62-16 du 24 mai 1962.

English gloss: the law sets the legal regime for renewable power projects in three forms:
self-consumption, supply to the domestic market, and export. It applies notwithstanding the
1962 decree-law that created STEG.

JORT p. 928, Art. 8:

> Le producteur d'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables prend en charge toutes les dépenses relatives au raccordement de l'unité de production au réseau électrique national, ainsi que les frais de renforcement du réseau électrique national si cela est rendu nécessaire pour l'opération d'évacuation de l'énergie électrique qu'il produit.

English gloss: the producer pays all grid connection costs, and any grid reinforcement needed to
evacuate its output.

JORT p. 928, Art. 9:

> Toute collectivité locale ou établissement public ou privé opérant dans les secteurs de l'industrie, de l'agriculture ou du tertiaire peut produire de l'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables à titre individuel à des fins d'autoconsommation. Ces organismes bénéficient du droit de transporter l'électricité produite à travers le réseau électrique national vers les centres de consommation, et du droit de vendre les excédents exclusivement à l'organisme public dans les limites d'un taux maximum, et ce, dans le cadre d'un contrat type approuvé par le ministre chargé de l'énergie.

English gloss: local authorities and industrial, agricultural or service entities may produce
for their own use. They may carry the power over the national grid to their sites, and sell
surplus only to the public utility, up to a maximum share.

JORT p. 928, Art. 12:

> La production d'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables pour répondre aux besoins de la consommation locale est soumise à une autorisation délivrée par le ministre chargé de l'énergie sur avis de la commission technique, et ce, dans la limite d'une puissance électrique maximale installée fixée par décret gouvernemental.
> Les contrats de production et de vente de l'électricité produite à partir des énergies renouvelables pour répondre aux besoins de la consommation locale sont soumis à la commission spéciale à l'Assemblé des représentants du peuple, accompagnés d'une copie de l'accord de principe, de l'autorisation définitive et des procès-verbaux de constat.
> L'octroi des autorisations intervient après la publication d'un avis annuel fixant les besoins nationaux en énergies renouvelables, émanant du ministre chargé de l'énergie.

English gloss: projects selling to the domestic market below a capacity ceiling need a
ministerial authorisation. Their contracts go to a special committee of parliament.
Authorisations are granted only after an annual notice of national needs.

JORT p. 928, Art. 13:

> Les projets de production d'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables pour satisfaire les besoins de la consommation locale, qui dépassent la puissance électrique maximale installée prévue à l'article 12 de la présente loi, sont réalisés conformément aux principes de la concurrence, de l'égalité des chances et de la transparence conformément à la législation en vigueur en matière d'attribution des concessions par l'Etat.
> Les contrats d'investissement y afférents sont soumis à la commission spéciale à l'assemblée des représentants du peuple. Les conventions conclues en ce qui concerne ces contrats sont soumises à l'assemblée pour approbation.

English gloss: projects above the ceiling go through competitive concessions, and their
agreements must be approved by parliament.

JORT p. 929, Art. 22:

> Le producteur d'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables vend l'électricité produite exclusivement et en totalité à l'organisme public qui s'engage à l'acheter, et ce, dans le cadre d'un contrat de vente conclu entre les deux parties conformément à un contrat type approuvé par arrêté du ministre chargé de l'énergie, déterminant notamment les conditions techniques et commerciales relatives à l'achat de l'électricité produite à partir des énergies renouvelables.
> Les prix d'achat sont fixés et révisés périodiquement chaque fois qu'il est jugé nécessaire, par arrêté du ministre chargé de l'énergie.

English gloss: authorised producers sell all their output, and only, to the public utility
under a standard contract. Purchase prices are set and revised by ministerial order.

JORT p. 929, Art. 24:

> Les projets de production d'électricité à partir des énergies renouvelables pour l'exportation sont réalisés dans le cadre de contrats de concession tout en tenant compte des besoins nationaux en énergie renouvelable.

JORT p. 930, Art. 25:

> Le contrat de concession est approuvé par loi.

English gloss: export projects are carried out by concession, and the concession contract is
approved by a law.

> يعتبر إحداث هيئة تعديلية للكهرباء من اوكد مطالب المستثمرين لتوضيح المسائل المتعلقة بالأسعار ووضع حدّ لمسالة تداخل الأدوار، حيث تضطلع الشركة التونسية للكهرباء بدور هام في هذا المجال وهو مال لا يتماشى مع قواعد الحوكمة والشفافية والممارسات الحسنة المعمول بها في هذا المجال. وتجدر الإشارة الى أنه تم اعداد مشروع قانون لإحداث هيئة تعديلية وتم عرضه على الاستشارة العمومية وهو حاليا جاهز للنشر.

English gloss: procedures take at least three years before production starts. Projects need
about 3 million dinars per MW under project finance, where the banks' main security is the
power purchase contract with STEG as sole and exclusive buyer; many investors asked for a
comfort letter, and comfort letters were issued in August 2022. Some newcomers bid very low
prices for speculation or from inexperience, and their projects then failed to reach financing;
the ministry is reforming the system by setting tariffs itself and screening project readiness
(bank approval, permits, site, bank guarantee) and revising the standard contract. The ageing
transmission grid is one of the main obstacles, and long connection procedures are a barrier.
Social acceptance is a major challenge in the economic crisis: nearby residents expect many
jobs, and land problems partly stem from local communities not being involved in energy
transition policy. Investors' most urgent demand is an electricity regulator, to clarify prices
and end overlapping roles, since STEG's large role does not fit good governance and transparency
practice; a draft law creating a regulator went through public consultation and is ready.

Policy paper by a German liberal political foundation, written with two ministry officials,
so it is close to the ministry's own account. It describes problems but gives few figures on
how many projects were delayed or by how long. Prices in millimes are converted by the author.
The 35% target here differs from the 30% in the 2015 Solar Plan text (SRC-TG-192) and the 2023

> The GoT plans to reach 35% of renewable energy in the electricity system capacity by 2030, against 3% currently.

> Renewable energy is then expected to cover 50% of the electricity needs by 2035, and 100% of all electricity needs by 2050.

English gloss: the government plans 35% renewables in electricity system capacity by 2030,
against 3% "currently", 50% of electricity needs by 2035 and 100% by 2050.

> The first major photovoltaic concession was granted in 2021, while the technical support in the form of an online bidding tool, review of bidding documents, and improved tendering manuals have helped to improve private sector confidence and responded to their concerns.

> Under the concession regime, the World Bank is helping to enhance the bidding documents for the call for proposals for 1,700 MW of solar and wind energy in 2022.

> The scale-up of renewable energy in Tunisia will depend on the availability of financing and the existence of profitable opportunities to attract the necessary private investments.

English gloss: the first large PV concession was granted in 2021; a 1,700 MW solar and wind call
for proposals followed in 2022; scale-up depends on financing and profitable opportunities.

> High energy costs have also contributed to the growing financial deficits of the state-owned enterprises (SOEs) working in the energy sector.
> Consequently, these effects make it more difficult to attract private investment to the energy sector, particularly for renewable energy.

English gloss: the growing deficits of energy-sector state enterprises make private investment,
especially in renewables, harder to attract.
resolvedSources.notes:
Quotes checked against the raw HTML of the page (tags stripped). The brief states the 2030 target as a share of system
capacity, not of generation; other sources state it as a share of generation (SRC-TG-192,
SRC-TG-103) or of the "energy mix" (SRC-TG-105). Its "3% currently" is not dated and does not
match IRENA's 15% of capacity in 2024 (SRC-TG-190) or ONEM's 8% of the STEG + IPP fleet in 2025
(SRC-TG-193); it may be an old generation share.

resolvedSources.title: Énergies Renouvelables : la Tunisie plafonne à 9,2 %, alors que les 35 % sont visés dès 2030
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article dated 8 September 2026, body text:

> Selon l'Observatoire national de l'énergie et des mines, les renouvelables ont représenté 9,2 % de la production électrique à fin juin 2026 , autoproduction comprise.

> Dès 2015 , la mise à jour du Plan solaire tunisien prévoyait de porter les renouvelables à 30 % de la production électrique en 2030 .

> Le gouvernement avait ensuite adopté le plan en juillet 2016, avec une étape intermédiaire de 12 % dès 2020 .

> Le bilan énergétique officiel pour 2020 évaluait alors la part des renouvelables à seulement 3,1 % de la production nationale d'électricité.

> Depuis, l'objectif final est devenu encore plus ambitieux : l'ANME affiche désormais 35 % de renouvelables dans la production électrique en 2030 .

> Le constat dressé mardi par Malken Kesksi , membre du Groupement professionnel des énergies renouvelables de la CONECT, est difficile à contester : la Tunisie avance, mais beaucoup trop lentement au regard de ses propres engagements.

English gloss: per ONEM, renewables were 9.2% of power generation at end June 2026, including
self-production. The 2015 Solar Plan update aimed at 30% of generation in 2030; the government
adopted it in July 2016 with an interim step of 12% in 2020. The official 2020 energy balance put
renewables at 3.1% of generation. ANME now states 35% of generation in 2030. A member of the
renewable energy group of the employers' body CONECT said Tunisia is progressing far too slowly.
resolvedSources.notes:
Press article, tier C, quoting ONEM, ANME and an industry representative. Its 12% interim
target for 2020 differs from the 14% in the Solar Plan text itself (SRC-TG-192, p. 9). Its 3.1%
for 2020 differs from the 2.6% computable from ONEM's key figures excluding self-producers
(SRC-TG-194); the article's figure may include self-production. The ANME 35% "of generation"
claim was not found in an ANME document.
